cases.histology: This neoplasm is composed of solid nests of uniform epithelioid cells with speckled chromatin and granular eosinophilic cytoplasm. The neoplasm has an infiltrative pattern of growth, as it permeates around bronchial cartilage. The neoplastic cells demonstrate diffuse immunoreactivity for cytokeratin AE1/3 and neuroendocrine markers chromogranin and synaptophysin. While the cells are cytologically bland, the mitotic rate is elevated at approximately 5 per 2mm2 squared. The Ki67 is 7%. Despite the absence of tumor necrosis, these features qualify for an atypical carcinoid tumor.
cases.discussion: Atypical carcinoid tumors have a mitotic rate of <2 per 2mm2 square (approximately 8 high power fields on most modern microscopes). Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma would demonstrate greater necrosis, and a mitotic rate of >10 per 2mm squared. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma typically has a neuroendocrine architecture (nested pattern with palisading of tumor nuclei at the edges) but cytology which is non neuroendocrine (open chromatin with fairly prominent nucleoli). Small cell carcinoma would similarly demonstrate necrosis and a high mitotic rate (>10 per 2mm2 squared, and usually far more than that). The neoplastic cells of small cell carcinoma have hyperchromatic chromatin and the nuclei mold to each other.

cases.source_answer: D. Papillary urothelial neoplasm with extensive denudation
cases.correct_answer: Papillary urothelial neoplasm with extensive denudation
cases.canonical_answer: Papillary urothelial neoplasm with extensive denudation
choices_raw: D. Papillary urothelial neoplasm with extensive denudation
choices: Papillary urothelial neoplasm with extensive denudation
cases.histology: Sections show a segment of urethra with a complex branching intraluminal exophytic proliferation of fibrovascular cores and stroma.
cases.discussion: Papillary urothelial neoplasms, particularly if high-grade, can become virtually entirely denuded such that all that is available for histologic review is the residual stromal skeleton devoid of neoplastic cells. The delicate, complex, branching architecture is still essentially diagnostic of a papillary urothelial neoplasm. Grading is difficult without associated tumor cells, but due to their frequent discohesion, such tumors often represent high grade papillary urothelial carcinoma. The current case was such an example, as the clinical history was notable for high-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma in the bladder with recurrent urethral tumors, and other sections from the same urethrectomy specimen showed non-invasive high grade papillary urothelial carcinoma. Nephrogenic adenoma can have papillary architecture but typically lacks such extensive branching and architectural complexity and would demonstrate bland cuboidal lining. Polypoid urethritis (or cystitis) is a tumor like lesion that can mimic an epithelial neoplasm but the lesion is mass forming due to underlying edema and fibrosis of the lamina propria rather than due to epithelial proliferation. Granulation tissue could look similar at very high magnification but is composed of an orderly arrangement of capillaries and fibrous tissue rather than a mass lesion with a delicate papillary configuration.

choices_raw: A. Intraductal carcinoma of the prostate
C. High grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia
cases.histology: Sections show a dense cribriform glandular epithelial proliferation but without cytologic atypia.
cases.discussion: Clear cell cribriform hyperplasia is an architectural mimicker of either Atypical intraductal proliferation or Intraductal carcinoma of the prostate, but the lack of nuclear atypia distinguishes this as a benign entity of no clinical significance. Architecturally, there is sufficient density of the epithelium to warrant a diagnosis of intraductal carcinoma, but that entity requires cytologic atypia or necrosis in addition to dense cribriform architecture. The term Atypical intraductal proliferation is typically used for lesions with some but not all the features of Intraductal carcinoma of the prostate. Such lesions show either cribriform growth but with “loose” architecture such that the quantity of epithelium does not definitively exceed that of the luminal spaces, or cytologic atypia beyond that typically seen in High grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia but not overtly malignant cytology to warrant a diagnosis of Intraductal carcinoma of the prostate. High grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia shows cytologic atypia analogous to that of invasive prostatic adenocarcinoma, but cribriform architecture is no longer accepted in High grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia with most lesions previously diagnosed as such likely qualifying as either Atypical intraductal proliferation or Intraductal carcinoma of the prostate by current criteria.

D. Papillary urothelial neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential / PUNLMP
choices: Papillary urothelial neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential / PUNLMP
cases.histology: Sections show a urothelial neoplasm with entirely inverted growth but without urothelial thickening, cytologic atypia, or invasion.
cases.discussion: This case exemplifies the key diagnostic features of inverted urothelial papilloma: lack of an exophytic papillary component, thin nests composed of non-thickened urothelial without cytologic atypia. Peripheral palisading is often present. The distinction of Inverted urothelial papilloma from the other listed entities is clinically significant as this lesion is entirely benign whereas the others all require long term follow-up due to the risk for multifocality and recurrence inherent to all exophytic urothelial neoplasms. Urothelial papilloma is exophytic and is composed of delicate papillary fronds projecting into the urinary space. Non-invasive low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma can have extensive inverted growth but this diagnosis requires cytologic atypia and/or altered polarity. Almost all urothelial carcinomas with inverted growth also have an exophytic component. Also, the inverted component of urothelial carcinomas typically have broad nests, reflecting the thickened urothelium of the underlying carcinoma. PUNLMP is an exophytic urothelial neoplasm composed of urothelium too thick for the diagnosis of a papilloma but without sufficient alteration in polarity or cytologic atypia to merit a designation of low grade papillary urothelial carcinoma.

cases.source_answer: D. Complete hydatidiform mole arising in a mosaic conception
cases.correct_answer: Complete hydatidiform mole arising in a mosaic conception
cases.canonical_answer: Complete hydatidiform mole arising in a mosaic conception
choices_raw: C. Non-molar abortus with some abnormal villous morphology, possibly related to trisomy
D. Complete hydatidiform mole arising in a mosaic conception
choices: Non-molar abortus with some abnormal villous morphology, possibly related to trisomy
Complete hydatidiform mole arising in a mosaic conception
cases.histology: The villi show basically two different populations, with some blending or merging of these. This includes one set with variably hydropically enlarged villi with some cisterns but no trophoblastic hyperplasia and another set with some modest trophoblastic hyperplasia. The latter is somewhat subtle and therefore challenging to appreciate.
cases.discussion:
This is an example of a complete hydatidiform mole arising in an androgenetic/biparental mosaic conception. Immunohistochemical analysis of p57 expression is quite useful for assisting in recognizing this uncommon entity, particularly when the molar component is somewhat subtle as in this case, and avoiding misclassification of the presence of two populations of villi as a partial hydatidiform mole. The p57 immunostain demonstrate that there are two different expression patterns. The dysmorphic villi that lack trophoblastic hyperplasia have a discordant pattern of p57 expression, manifested as positive nuclear expression in the cytotrophoblastic cell layer and negative in the villous stromal cells. In contrast, in the villi with some trophoblastic hyperplasia both of these cell types are negative. A partial hydatidiform mole would have uniform p57 expression in both of these cell populations. If these different villous populations can be separately genotyped, the p57-negative component will demonstrate a purely androgenetic pattern, consistent with a complete hydatidiform mole component, and the p57-discordant component will demonstrate a biparental pattern with allele ratios enriched for the paternal allele, indicating a mixture of androgenetic (p57-) and biparental (p57+) cells.

Reference: Lewis GH, DeScipio C, Murphy KM, Haley L, Beierl K, Mosier S, Tandy S, Cohen DS, Lytwyn A, Elit L, Vang R, Ronnett BM. Characterization of androgenetic/biparental mosaic/chimeric conceptions, including some with a molar component: morphology, p57 immunohistochemistry, molecular genotyping, and risk of persistent gestational trophoblastic disease. Int J Gynecol Pathol 2013;32(2):199-214.

references.text: Lewis GH, DeScipio C, Murphy KM, Haley L, Beierl K, Mosier S, Tandy S, Cohen DS, Lytwyn A, Elit L, Vang R, Ronnett BM. cases.attribution: Case presented by Dr. Brigitte Ronnett, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
cases.vignette: This case is a 34 year old female with hemoperitoneum, clinically assessed as a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, with HCG >200,000, and an enlarged ovary disrupted by clot.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Brigitte Ronnett, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This case is a 34 year old female with hemoperitoneum, clinically assessed as a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, with HCG >200,000, and an enlarged ovary disrupted by clot.
cases.histology: The ovary has a hypercellular sheet-like mass with morphologically distinct yet intimately admixed cell populations. This proliferation is comprised of different types of trophoblastic cells, including cytotrophoblast—the monotonous mononucleated cells with clear cytoplasm cells and readily evident mitotic figures--and syncytiotrophoblast—the multinucleated cells with abundant eosinophilic to amphophilic cytoplasm. The tumor displays the characteristic pattern of syncytiotrophoblastic cells wrapping around aggregates of cytotrophoblast.
cases.discussion:
This morphology is classical choriocarcinoma. In women, there are various types of choriocarcinoma. These include gestational, germ cell, and somatic types. The most common type occurs within the uterus as a gestational type of tumor. This is most commonly related to a complete hydatidiform mole, which can be an antecedent pregnancy event (recent or even years before) or a concurrent one. However, gestational choriocarcinoma can also occur in a non-molar pregnancy, more commonly as intraplacental choriocarcinoma in the term or near-term setting but also early in a non-molar pregnancy. Choriocarcinoma of germ cell type, whether pure or mixed with other germ cell components, is rare in the ovary. The somatic type is a tumor comprised of some kind of carcinoma, often an adenocarcinoma, with a component having choriocarcinomatous differentiation arising from that carcinomatous component. When in the ovary and occurring as pure choriocarcinoma--lacking other germ cell components or somatic carcinoma components—the differential diagnosis concerns a metastasis from a uterine gestational choriocarcinoma, a rare ectopic ovarian gestational choriocarcinoma, or a rare ovarian choriocarcinoma of germ cell type. Genotyping can distinguish gestational tumors from non-gestational tumors (germ cell and somatic tumors). Gestational choriocarcinoma is purely androgenetic when related to a molar pregnancy and is biparental when related to a non-molar conception. Both germ cell and somatic types of choriocarcinoma have genotypes that match the patient DNA. Molecular testing of this tumor demonstrated that the choriocarcinoma was biparental, consistent with a tumor of gestational rather than of germ cell or somatic type. The biparental genotype indicated that this was the less common gestational type derived from an early non-molar conception rather than the more common molar-associated androgenetic type. There was no evidence of an intrauterine pregnancy, so this is a rare gestational choriocarcinoma arising as an ectopic ovarian pregnancy unrelated to a complete hydatidiform mole.

Reference: Savage J, Adams E, Veras E, Murphy KM, Ronnett BM. Choriocarcinoma in women: analysis of a case series with genotyping. Am J Surg Pathol 2017;41(12):1593-1606.

references.text: Savage J, Adams E, Veras E, Murphy KM, Ronnett BM. Choriocarcinoma in women: analysis of a case series with genotyping. Am J Surg Pathol 2017;41(12):1593-1606.

Choriocarcinoma of germ cell type, whether pure or mixed with other germ cell components, is rare in the ovary. The somatic type is a tumor comprised of some kind of carcinoma, often an adenocarcinoma, with a component having choriocarcinomatous differentiation arising from that carcinomatous component. When in the ovary and occurring as pure choriocarcinoma--lacking other germ cell components or somatic carcinoma components—the differential diagnosis concerns a metastasis from a uterine gestational choriocarcinoma, a rare ectopic ovarian gestational choriocarcinoma, or a rare ovarian choriocarcinoma of germ cell type. Genotyping can distinguish gestational tumors from non-gestational tumors (germ cell and somatic tumors). Gestational choriocarcinoma is purely androgenetic when related to a molar pregnancy and is biparental when related to a non-molar conception. Both germ cell and somatic types of choriocarcinoma have genotypes that match the patient DNA. Molecular testing of this tumor demonstrated that the choriocarcinoma was biparental, consistent with a tumor of gestational rather than of germ cell or somatic type. The biparental genotype indicated that this was the less common gestational type derived from an early non-molar conception rather than the more common molar-associated androgenetic type. There was no evidence of an intrauterine pregnancy, so this is a rare gestational choriocarcinoma arising as an ectopic ovarian pregnancy unrelated to a complete hydatidiform mole.

cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Jacqueline Birkness-Gartman, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This case is an elderly female with a liver mass.
cases.histology: Sections show a neoplasm consisting of sheets of cells with eosinophilic to clear cytoplasm, nuclear pleomorphism, necrosis, and mitotic activity.
cases.discussion: All of the diagnoses listed are reasonable considerations. We initially considered hepatocellular carcinoma given that the lesion was designated as a liver mass, but the degree of atypia is greater than that which we typically see and liver markers (HepPar-1, arginase, in situ hybridization for albumin) were negative. Additional immunostains showed that the neoplasm was positive for synaptophysin, focally positive for cytokeratin AE1/3 and Cam5.2, and negative for chromogranin, S100, Melan-A, HMB45, and SMA. Given the morphology and immunolabeling profile, adrenocortical carcinoma was subsequently considered. Immunostains for inhibin and SF-1 were strongly positive, supporting this diagnosis. The patient's history was further investigated, and it turned out that this lesion was actually a large mass involving both the liver and adrenal gland.

cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Jacqueline Birkness-Gartman, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This case is an adult female who was pregnant with appendicitis.
cases.histology: Sections show a proliferation of eosinophilic cells with abundant cytoplasm, extending from the serosal surface to the submucosa of the appendix.
cases.discussion:
This is an exuberant example of deciduosis (decidualized endometrial stroma) involving the appendix. On immunostains, the decidualized cells were negative for CD68, S100, and AE1/3, while positive for CD10 and PR. Deciduosis typically affects young women, who may be pregnant or taking oral contraceptives. Appendiceal deciduosis can present as acute appendicitis, and extra-appendiceal involvement is seen in 43% of cases, according to one study.

Reference: Noor M, Chen A, Gonzalez RS. Clinicopathologic findings in gynecologic proliferations of the appendix. Hum Pathol. 2019 Oct;92:101-106.

cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Jacqueline Birkness-Gartman, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This case is an adult female who had an appendectomy.
choices_raw: B. Low grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm (LAMN)
cases.histology: Sections show an appendectomy with glands and mucin involving the muscularis propria and peri-appendiceal adipose tissue. Many of the glands are lined by columnar epithelial cells without intracytoplasmic mucin, and surrounded by a spindled stroma. At the tip of the appendix, the cells lining the glands have intracytoplasmic mucin, but similar stroma is seen.
cases.discussion:
This is an example of intestinal metaplasia in endometriosis, and is a potential diagnostic pitfall, as the findings could mimic a low grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm (LAMN). A CD10 stain highlighted the endometrial stroma in the more classic foci of endometriosis, as well as the area with intestinal metaplasia. Of note, while endometriosis without intestinal metaplasia will be positive for CK7 and ER in the epithelium, endometriosis with intestinal metaplasia will instead express CDX-2. Identification and immunolabeling of the stroma is therefore helpful for reaching the correct diagnosis.

Reference: Vyas M, Wong S, Zhang X. Intestinal metaplasia of appendiceal endometriosis is not uncommon and may mimic appendiceal mucinous neoplasm. Pathol Res Pract. 2017;213(1):39-44.

choices_raw: B. Somatic malignancy arising from a mixed germ cell tumor
choices: Somatic malignancy arising from a mixed germ cell tumor
cases.histology: Within a lymph node, there is a well-circumscribed mass forming sheets and nests of dyscohesive tumor cells separated by fibrous septae. The tumor cells are hyperchromatic and have enlarged pleomorphic nuclei with dispersed chromatin and numerous mitotic figures. There is the suggestion of rosetting.
cases.discussion:
This is a somatic malignancy arising from a mixed germ cell tumor. The patient had a history of a mixed germ cell tumor. On H&E, no typical germ cell tumor morphology could be appreciated (seminoma, yolk sac tumor, embryonal carcinoma, teratoma). Immunostains could identify different germ cell tumors. First-line germ cell markers would include OCT3/4, CD30, glypican-3, hCG, and cytokeratin. The tumor was negative for all markers tested. The possibility of a somatic malignancy arising from the teratoma component of the known mixed germ cell tumor was then considered. The most common histologies are rhabdomyosarcoma, adenocarcinoma, neuroectodermal type tumors, and other sarcomas, however, IHC was not supportive of any specific histologic type. In this situation, isochrome 12p or overexpression of 12p can support germ cell origin, which was identified in this case.

Reference: Lobo J, Costa AL, Vilela-Salgueiro B, Rodrigues Â, Guimarães R, Cantante M, Lopes P, Antunes L, Jerónimo C, Henrique R. Testicular germ cell tumors: revisiting a series in light of the new WHO classification and AJCC staging systems, focusing on challenges for pathologists. Hum Pathol. 2018 Dec;82:113-124.

This case is an elderly male with an atrial mass.
cases.histology: Paucicellular tissue with papillary excrescences is lined by atypical epithelioid cells. There are large adjacent areas of necrosis and fibrin.
cases.discussion:
This is a metastatic carcinoma colonizing the surface of the atrium. Immunohistochemistry was performed and showed that the malignant cells labeled for CK20, claudin4, and CDX2. Mesothelial markers TTF-1 and p40 were negative. The pattern was suggestive of lower GI tract origin.

Metastases are 30x more common than primary neoplasms of the heart. The incidence of metastases to the heart has been increasing in recent years. Reported metastasis to the heart include lung, stomach, ovary, colon, liver or kidney carcinomas. Metastasis to the right side of the heart is more common than to the left side.

cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Elizabeth Thompson, MD, PhD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This case is a female child with a scalp mass.
cases.histology: There are skin and adnexal structures supporting location is the scalp. The lesion under the skin consists of cystic spaces and nodules with abundant giant cells. There are rims of basaloid cells at the base of nodules blending into eosinophilic “ghost cells”.
cases.discussion: This is a pilomatrixoma, which is a benign dermal or subcutaneous tumor that shows differentiation toward hair follicle matrix that is common in children and young adults. The nodule is typically solitary, deep, slow-growing, can be cystic, and localize in the head, neck, and upper extremities. Upon gross examination, they appear to be firm nodules with variegated, chalky, gray-brown or yellow-white color. Microscopically, the lesion contains sheets of basaloid epithelial cells, eosinophilic “ghost cells”, and intervening stroma that contain foreign body giant cells and inflammation. Nodules of calcification and ossification can occur. These tumors are most often sporadic and sporadic pilomatricomas can harbor activating mutations in beta-catenin. cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Andres Matoso, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This case is an adult male with a testicular tumor.
cases.histology: The lesion is a basaloid mass with prominent vasculature with large epithelioid cells that are falling apart. The nuclei have speckled chromatin, large nucleoli, and lots of mitosis. The background testis has spermatogenesis arrest.
cases.discussion:
This is a metastatic melanoma to the testes. When thinking about a blue cell tumor in the testis, there are a wide range of poorly or undifferentiated tumors to consider in the differential. Examples of tumors and their stains include: carcinomas (keratins), lymphomas (CD45), and sarcomas such as rhabdomyosarcoma (desmin, myogenin). Other tumors to consider include sex cord stromal tumor, such as a Leydig cell tumor (SF1, inhibin), embryonal carcinoma (OCT3/4, CD30, keratin), Sertoli cell (SF1, GATA4), yolk sac tumor (Glypican3, CDX2), carcinoid (synaptophysin/chromogranin), vascular tumors (CD34, CD31), and Ewings sarcoma (CD99). In this case, all of the immunostains for these malignancies were negative. If stains are negative for every malignancy, think about metastatic melanoma in the differential.
Metastatic melanoma is spread of melanoma from a cutaneous or extra-cutaneous primary melanoma to sites beyond the skin and subcutaneous fat. Approximately 60-80% of patients with metastatic melanoma have involvement of regional lymph nodes. Other sites of metastasis include distant nodes, lungs, liver, brain, bone, and intestine, with testes as a possible location as well.

cases.vignette: This case is an elderly female with a kidney tumor.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Andres Matoso, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This case is an elderly female with a kidney tumor.
choices_raw: D. Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
cases.histology: The lesion is an unencapsulated, well-circumscribed eosinophilic mass with prominent cystic spaces. The cells appear hobnailed and cribriform with fibrotic stroma. Nucleoli are large.
cases.discussion:
This is a tubulocystic renal cell carcinoma (TcRCC), which is a rare cystic renal epithelial neoplasm with exclusive tubulocystic growth. The tumor is found in the renal cortex and corticomedullar junction. This is an exceedingly rare tumor representing <1% of renal tumors. The median age of patients with this tumor are 58.4 years (ranging from 30-74) and there is a male predominance. Mutations in ABL1 and PDGFRA have been reported in a few cases. Upon gross examination, TcRCC is well circumscribed as a solitary mass with a spongy appearance and a cut surface with small white cysts with clear fluid. Microscopically, there are small tubules admixed with larger cysts lined by flat, cuboidal, and hobnail epithelium. The nuclei are enlarged with prominent nucleoli and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.
Low-grade fumarate hydratase (FH)-deficient tumors must be excluded by immunohistochemistry. They are cognized by their heterogeneous architecture and high-grade features. FH deficiency tumors have a high chance of being syndromic. Immunostains showing fumarate hydratase loss of staining and staining of endothelium as an internal control can confirm FH deficiency. S-(2-succino)-cysteine (2SC) is another useful stain that will be positively overexpressed in FH deficient tumors. A pure tubulocystic renal cell carcinoma typically is indolent and has a good prognosis, with rare reports of metastasis.

Reference: Amin MB, MacLennan GT, Gupta R, Grignon D, Paraf F, Vieillefond A, Paner GP, Stovsky M, Young AN, Srigley JR, Cheville JC. Tubulocystic carcinoma of the kidney: clinicopathologic analysis of 31 cases of a distinctive rare subtype of renal cell carcinoma. Am J Surg Pathol. 2009 Mar;33(3):384-92.

cases.vignette: This case is an elderly male with a testicular tumor.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Andres Matoso, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This case is an elderly male with a testicular tumor.
cases.histology: The lesion is within the testis and consists of a fibrous mass next to vessels and containing lymphocytic aggregates. There are epithelioid cells with cytoplasmic vacuoles in large tubule-like structures that are infiltrative between seminiferous tubules. On high power, the cells have a bland cytomorphology.
cases.discussion:
An adenomatoid tumor is a benign neoplasm of mesothelial origin displaying a spectrum of tubular, nested, or cord-like patterns. Commonly, they are in a paratesticular location and most often arise from the epididymis and can grow between seminiferous tubules and into testicular parenchyma. Adenomatoid tumors account for 1/3 of all adnexal tumor and 60% of benign adnexal tumors. Although these tumors are most predominant in patients 40 years old, they have been described in all age groups. In terms of etiology, there has been an association between immunosuppression in patients undergoing treatment for autoimmune diseases or after allograft organ transplants and the development of these tumors. This association suggests that immune dysregulation within mesothelial cells could contribute to tumor formation. Upon gross examination, these tumors are well-circumscribed round to oval masses with a white or tan surface. Microscopically, these tumors are rounded nodules with proliferating gland-like or vascular-like spaces lined by columnar layer of neoplastic cells. Intracytoplasmic vacuolization is observed. In addition, the background stroma is fibrous or collagenous with scattered lymphoid aggregates present. Infarcted tumors may show have regenerative changes. Immunohistochemical stains may be helpful with pancytokeratin, CAM5.2, CK7, calretinin, WT1, HBME1, BAP1, L1CMA, and podoplanin positivity. Surgical resection is curative.

Reference: Sangoi AR, McKenney JK, Schwartz EJ, Rouse RV, Longacre TA. Adenomatoid tumors of the female and male genital tracts: a clinicopathological and immunohistochemical study of 44 cases. Mod Pathol. 2009 Sep;22(9):1228-35.

cases.vignette: This is a 30 year old female with a leg mass.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This is a 30 year old female with a leg mass.
choices_raw: B. Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor
cases.histology: This is a post-treatment specimen, but the characteristic features of the neoplasm are retained. The predominance of the neoplasm is composed of plump spindle cells forming sheets with a prominent staghorn (hemangiopericytomatous) vasculature. Some areas of the tumor are extremely cellular with prominent mitotic activity, whereas others are associated with less cellularity and more abundant collagen deposition in association with dilated vessels. Some portions of the tumor have a more round cell appearance with less spindling. The neoplasm demonstrates strong nuclear labeling for TLE1 protein, and demonstrated the characteristic SS18-SSX1 gene fusion of synovial sarcoma.
cases.discussion: Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) may overlap significantly with synovial sarcoma, as both may be biphasic and dominated by spindle cells forming poorly formed fascicles. MPNST typically demonstrates greater cytologic atypia than synovial sarcoma (which is a translocation associated cancer) and is frequently associated with nerve trunks and/or a history of neurofibromatosis type 1. Solitary fibrous tumor may overlap cytologically with synovial sarcoma, in that both are composed of plump spindle cells without significant pleomorphism. Both are associated with dilated “hemangiopericytomatous” vasculature and collagen deposition. Solitary fibrous tumor should not label for TLE 1, but instead labels for STAT6. It is associated with a NAB2-STAT6 gene fusion which is distinct from the gene fusion of synovial sarcoma. Ewing sarcoma is suggested by the more round cell (poorly differentiated) areas of the current neoplasm. However, the spindling and collagen deposition as well hemangiopericytomatous vasculature seen in the current specimen are much more typical of synovial sarcoma than Ewing sarcoma, which is prototypical small round cell neoplasm. Ewing sarcoma demonstrates the typical EWSR1-FLI1 gene fusion or variants thereof which are distinct from the synovial sarcoma gene fusion.

cases.vignette: This is a 68 year old female with a liver mass. A previous biopsy of the tumor demonstrated immunoreactivity for synaptophysin.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This is a 68 year old female with a liver mass. A previous biopsy of the tumor demonstrated immunoreactivity for synaptophysin.
cases.histology: This is a solid cellular neoplasm with a prominent capillary vasculature. The nuclei are generally uniform. The chromatin is evenly distributed, raising the possibility of a metastatic neuroendocrine neoplasm from the gastrointestinal tract. Indeed, this is most likely diagnosis based on the morphologic features alone. However, focally one can appreciate a smaller population of basophilic cells which have less cytoplasm. Also, one can focally appreciate follicular architecture, with the neoplastic cells surrounding pink secretions similar to the pattern seen in a thyroid follicular neoplasm. No prior history of neuroendocrine neoplasm of the GI tract or elsewhere was obtained in the patient, and there was no history of breast carcinoma. The neoplasm demonstrated diffuse immunoreactivity for inhibin, as well as immunoreactivity for biliary cytokeratin 19. These are the hallmark features of what has been termed “cholangioblastic cholangiocarcinoma”.
cases.discussion: Well differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasm is the most common misdiagnosis for these cases. One helpful feature is that cholangioblastic cholangiocarcinomas do not label for INSM1, and typically have a higher mitotic rate than the usual grade 1 metastatic neuroendocrine neoplasm. Moreover, the absence of an identifiable primary outside of the liver should suggest this diagnosis. Metastatic breast carcinoma with endocrine differentiation is another significant consideration, particularly in women with a liver neoplasm demonstrating neuroendocrine differentiation but a higher grade than the usual grade 1 neuroendocrine neoplasm. cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This is a 1 week old female with a large renal mass.
cases.source_answer: A. Rhabdoid tumor of the kidney
choices_raw: A. Rhabdoid tumor of the kidney
cases.histology: The neoplastic cells are epithelioid to spindled, and permeate between native nephrons. Focally, the native renal tubules show primitive chromatin, mimicking the epithelial component of a nephroblastoma (embryonal hyperplasia). The neoplastic cells are focally spindled and are associated with collagen production. Mitotic activity is extremely high and there is prominent apoptosis. The neoplastic cells, where epithelioid, focally demonstrate the characteristic cytologic triad of vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and eccentric hyaline cytoplasm inclusions. These are the typical features of a rhabdoid tumor. The neoplasm demonstrates loss of INI1 protein (SMARCB4) by immunohistochemistry, supporting the diagnosis.
cases.discussion:
The cellular variant of congenital mesoblastic nephroma is the key differential in this young age group. In individual fields, the spindle cell areas of this neoplasm are virtually indistinguishable from a cellular congenital mesoblastic nephroma. However, a cellular congenital mesoblastic nephroma typically has a pushing pattern and does not typically contain native nephrons within it. The variation of cellularity of the current neoplasm would also be unusual for a cellular congenital mesoblastic nephroma, which is essentially infantile fibrosarcoma of the renal sinus. Cellular congenital mesoblastic nephroma would typically demonstrate the ETV6-NTRK3 gene fusion, as opposed to the INI1 loss seen in rhabdoid tumor. Wilms tumor may be mimicked by the focal embryonal hyperplasia of the entrapped nephrons, suggesting an epithelial component. The vesicular chromatin and prominent nucleoli of the current lesion would be highly atypical for a nephroblastoma. Also, another important morphologic feature is that the cytology of the entrapped tubules undergoing embryonal hyperplasia is different from that of the surrounding rhabdoid tumor: embryonal hyperplasia nuclei are condensed and basophilic, while the chromatin of the rhabdoid tumor surrounding these tubules is vesicular and the nucleus contains a prominent nucleolus. Synovial sarcoma may have poorly differentiated areas that resemble the current case; however, the age at presentation is completely different. Primary synovial sarcomas typically occur in young adults, while rhabdoid tumors typically occur in children under the age of 3 years. Synovial sarcoma would demonstrate the characteristic SS18-SSX1/SSX2 fusions that are the hallmark of that entity, and would not typically demonstrate loss of INI1.

Rhabdoid tumor of the kidney is a highly lethal cancer that effects very young children. A significant proportion of cases (approximately one third) prove to have germline INI1 alterations, predisposing the child to second malignancies such as atypical teratoid tumor of the central nervous system, and having potential familial implications.

references.text: Am J Surg Pathol. 1989 Jun;13(6):439-58. Crit Rev Oncog. 2015;20(3-4):199-216.

cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Ashley Cimino-Mathews, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This case is an adult male with an adrenal mass.
cases.histology: This lesion is located centrally in the adrenal gland and is composed of cells with abundant amphophilic, granular cytoplasm and a delicate capillary vasculature. The nuclei have evenly dispersed chromatin, variably pleomophic forms, and variably prominent nucleoli.
cases.discussion: This lesion is a pheochromoctyoma, which is a catecholamine-secreting neuroendocrine tumor arising from the central adrenal medulla. More than 40% of pheochromocytomas are hereditary and occur in patients demonstrating multiple tumors or presenting in childhood or before age 40. The clinical presentation of pheochromocytoma is largely related to the tumor’s production of catecholamines, which results in hypertension, tremor, headache, and palpitations. Grossly, pheochromocytomas have a tan cut surface with focal hemorrhage and areas of necrosis. The classic microscopic findings for pheochromocytoma are cells with amphophilic cytoplasm arranged in nests (“Zellballen” pattern) and with a delicate capillary vasculature. Pheochromocytoma label for immunostains for neuroendocrine differentiation, including synaptophysin, chromogranin, and INSM1. Notably, pheochromocytomas (as well as their extraadrenal counterpart, paragrangliomas) are negative for cytokeratin by immunohistochemistry, which distinguishes them from neuroendocrine tumors with epithelial differentiation (e.g., carcinoid tumor/well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors, neuroendocrine carcinomas, and neuroendocrine adenomas such as parathyroid adenoma).

cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Ashley Cimino-Mathews, MD and prepared by Dr. Annie A. Wu, MD, PhD.
This case is an adult male with a thyroid mass.
cases.histology: The lesion has two well-circumscribed nodules of the same entity. The smaller nodule contains epithelioid cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin and a nested architecture. The larger nodule contains spindle cells with a higher nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio, rendering them “darker” from low magnification, and a streaming architectural pattern.
cases.discussion: This is a medullary thyroid carcinoma, which is a malignant tumor of parafollicular C cell origin. Medullary thyroid carcinoma typically presents as a solitary nodule in the upper two-thirds of the lateral lobes. While invasion of surrounding structures can result in difficulty breathing or swallowing, the tumors typically come to clinical attention due to the high levels of calcitonin secreted from these tumors, which results in symptoms such as diarrhea, flushing, or weight loss. This malignancy accounts for 2% of all thyroid malignancies. Patients with sporadic medullary thyroid carcinoma typically present with unilateral disease at age 45-55 years old with a slight female predominance. The etiology of sporadic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unknown. Patients with hereditary medullary thyroid carcinoma present earlier at age 20-30 with multifocal and bilateral disease. The hereditary mutation is a gain-of-function in the RET protooncogene indicating MEN2A or MEN2B. Grossly, the tumors are well-circumscribed but unencapsulated with a tan-yellow color. Microscopically, the tumor cells can be arranged in solid nests separated by fibrous septae that may contain stromal amyloid deposition. In addition, medullary thyroid tumors can have a streaming architecture with spindle cells arranged in short intersecting fascicles. This pattern often seen in neoplasms with neuroendicrine differentiation, such as carcinoid tumors in the lung. In some cases, medullary tumors contain pleomorphic cells with bizarre nuclei, which is also typical of the “neuroendocrine atypia” seen in neuroendocrine tumors. Medullary carcinoma typically label diffusely with immunostains calcitonin and for neuroendocrine differentiation, including synaptophysin, chromogranin and INSM1. Medullary carcinomas are immunoreactive for TTF-1, which overlaps with the labeling of papillary thyroid carcinoma and follicular carcinoma, however, in contrast to the latter two, medullary carcinomas are negative for thyroglobulin and PAX8.

This case is an adult female with a mediastinal mass.
choices_raw: D. Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma
choices: Metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma
cases.histology: The lesion is a well-circumscribed encapsulated mass in thymic lymphoid structure with Hassle corpuscles. The mass contains sheets of monotonous round uniform cells with round salt and pepper nuclei. The cells are surrounded by pale, clear cytoplasm with distinct borders. There are no mitoses. The cells are surrounded by delicate vasculature and form pseudofollicles containing colloid-like secretions.
cases.discussion: This is a parathyroid adenoma, which is a benign parathyroid neoplasm composed of predominantly 1-2 cell types (chief, transitional oncocytic, oncocytic, or clear cells). Parathyroid adenomas typically arise in parathyroid glands, more frequently the inferior glands than superior glands. However, parathyroid adenomas can also occur in ectopic regions related to embryologic development. For instance, thymus, thyroid, and mediastinum are other potential locations of parathyroid adenoma occurrence. Up to 10% of parathyroid adenomas are hereditary, either as part of a syndrome, such as MEN (multiple endocrine neoplasia), or non-syndromic. A risk factor for parathyroid adenoma is neck radiation and external ionizing radiation exposure from atomic bombs or nuclear power plants. Grossly, parathyroid adenomas are ovoid pink or tan with delicate pseudocapsules and may contain fluid-filled cysts. Microscopically, most parathyroid adenomas are composed of chief cells often with a mixture of clear cells and oncophils. Immunohistochemically, parathyroid adenomas label for parathyroid hormone (PTH) and markers of neuroendocrine differentiation including synaptophysin, chromogranin and INSM1. They are negative for TTF-1 and thyroglobulin, which distinguishes them from thyroid, and they are negative for PAX8, which distinguishes them from thyroid and renal cell carcinoma.

cases.vignette: This is a 47 year old female with renal mass.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is a 47 year old female with renal mass.
cases.histology: The main lesion in this kidney is a solid epithelioid cell neoplasm with focal nested and corded architecture which strongly suggests epithelial differentiation. One clue to the diagnosis of the main tumor, however, it is the presence of incipient muscle predominant angiomyolipomas in the surrounding kidney. The main epithelioid lesion is completely negative for all cytokeratins and for PAX8, and demonstrates immunoreactivity for HMB45, Melan A, and cathepsin K in a patchy fashion. These are the findings of epithelioid angiomyolipoma. The current case has oncocytoma like morphology (which may account for the less than usual immunolabeling for melanocytic markers as the cells likely are filled with mitochondria), and also demonstrates cytologic atypia which indicates that close follow-up is indicated.
cases.discussion: Eosinophilic chromophobe renal cell carcinoma should demonstrate immunoreactivity for cytokeratin, and demonstrates edematous hyalinized stroma and irregular nuclei. Eosinophilic vacuolated tumor should label for cytokeratins, and demonstrates prominent cytoplasmic vacuolization not seen in the current case. Low grade oncocytic tumor labels diffusely for cytokeratin 7, should not label for melanocytic markers.

cases.vignette: This is an 85 year old female with renal mass.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is an 85 year old female with renal mass.
cases.histology: The neoplasm has solid architecture, and is composed of epithelioid cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and well defined cell borders. The nuclei have somewhat convoluted, raisinoid contours. The stromal vessels are hyalinized and relatively hypocellular. The neoplasm demonstrates immunoreactivity for CD117 and focal labeling for cytokeratin 7. The morphology and immunoprofile are consistent with eosinophilic chromophobe renal cell carcinoma.
cases.discussion: Oncocytoma typically has nested architecture within edematous stroma, and the nuclei are perfectly round without the irregularity seen in the current case. Low grade oncocytic tumors typically have solid architecture, but have central areas with linear cords of neoplastic cells within loose stroma (“boats in a bay”), and typically label for cytokeratin 7 but not CD117. Eosinophilic vacuolated tumor typically consists of eosinophilic polygonal cells with prominent cytoplasmic vacuolization, set in an edematous hyalinized stroma with thick walled vessels and calcification. These neoplasms typical label for CD117 but not for cytokeratin 7.

cases.title: Week 795: Case 1
cases.attribution: Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
cases.vignette: This is a 60 year old female with a renal/perirenal mass.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is a 60 year old female with a renal/perirenal mass.
cases.histology:
This malignant neoplasm is centered in the perirenal soft tissue. The majority of the neoplasm consists undifferentiated small round cells with abundant mitotic activity and necrosis. There is focal spindling. These cells have a nonspecific immunophenotype, with negative reactions for cytokeratin, CD99, S100, SF1, melanocytic markers, and CD34.

The best clue to the diagnosis of the case is the fat surrounding the high grade lesion. While much of it appears at first glance to be normal fat, one can appreciate focally the presence of enlarged hyperchromatic nuclei in the thin fibrous septa separating fat lobules. This is the typical morphology of well differentiated liposarcoma. The diagnosis is confirmed by strong nuclear immunoreactivity for MDM2 and positive in situ hybridization for MDM2 in the well differentiated liposarcomatous component and the high grade component, which thus constitutes dedifferentiated liposarcoma.
cases.discussion: Adrenal cortical carcinoma would typically label for SF1, typically features epithelioid eosinophilic cells, and lacks a lipomatous component. The primitive appearance of the neoplasm raised the possibility of Ewing sarcoma; however, the absence of immunoreactivity for CD99 as well as the lipomatous component helps exclude that diagnosis. Malignant solitary fibrous tumors may lose CD34 immunoreactivity and hence mimic primitive neoplasms such as Ewing sarcoma or (in the kidney) clear cell sarcoma, particularly since they overexpress BCOR protein (Am J Surg Pathol 2019; 43:773-782 PMID 30864973). However, the absence of immunoreactivity for STAT6 as well as the atypical lipomatous component helps exclude this diagnosis.

cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Jonathan I. Epstein and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
A 50 year-old man underwent a biopsy of a prostatic urethral lesion. There was no pertinent clinical history at the time of the consult. Outside stains were negative for NKX3.1, PSA, GATA3, p63, keratin 7 and PAX8. The lesion was diffusely positive for Keratin 20 and SATB2.
choices_raw: Villous adenoma with high grade dysplasia of the urethra
choices: Villous adenoma with high grade dysplasia of the urethra
cases.histology: A villous adenomatous lesion is present.
cases.discussion:
Colon carcinoma can involve the bladder either via direct invasion or metastases. Histologically, when colon adenocarcinomas involves the bladder it can either: 1) undermine the normal urothelium, which is a clue that the tumor is secondarily involving the bladder; 2) colonize the surface mimicking in situ adenocarcinoma; or 3) when the colon adenocarcinoma reaches the bladder luminal surface, there is a tendency to form papillary fronds of cancer that can be histologically indistinguishable from a primary villous adenoma of the bladder.

Colonic adenocarcinoma invading the bladder can also resemble prostatic ductal adenocarcinoma, unless there is more mucinous appearing epithelium which would be unusual for prostatic duct adenocarcinoma. Prostatic duct adenocarcinoma would be NKX3.1 positive, but can also express CDX2. Immunohistochemically, there is no way to distinguish colon carcinoma from bladder adenocarcinoma as both express CDX2 and SATB2. Nuclear beta-catenin would favor colon, but I still would rely on clinically ruling out a colon cancer. Patients with colon cancer invading the bladder may present with bladder involvement at the time of diagnosis of colon cancer or develop vesical lesions several years after resection of their colonic primary. The majority have genitourinary symptoms at presentation with gastrointestinal manifestations less common. The initial clinical impression, largely based on cystoscopic and radiographic studies, can either be a bladder primary or colon cancer.

Distinguishing a primary bladder adenocarcinoma from spread of a colonic carcinoma to the bladder may not be possible on histopathologic grounds alone. Consideration should be given to the possibility of an extravesical primary even when symptomatology, cystoscopy, radiographic studies, and histopathology suggest a primary bladder glandular neoplasm. There are a couple of situations where one can be more definitive that a glandular neoplasm in the bladder is primary at that site. One is if the villous adenoma or adenocarcinoma is arising in the setting of intestinal metaplasia. The other is in lesions arising in the dome of the bladder, which would favor urachal origin, and is not a typical site of spread from the intestines. In the current case, clinically there was a history of advanced colonic adenocarcinoma. In cases, without a history of colon carcinoma with a villous appearance, I will diagnose as: "Villous adenomatous lesion. See note:

Note: This lesion may be a primary villous adenoma of the bladder. However, colonic adenocarcinoma can involve the bladder mimicking a villous adenoma. Clinical correlation is required.”

Reference: Silver SA, Epstein JI. Adenocarcinoma of the colon simulating primary urinary bladder neoplasia. A report of nine cases. Am J Surg Pathol. 1993 Feb;17(2):171-8.

cases.vignette: A 63 year-old male underwent a partial nephrectomy of a 3.5 cm renal nodule.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Jonathan I. Epstein and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
A 63 year-old male underwent a partial nephrectomy of a 3.5 cm renal nodule.
choices_raw: Low grade oncocytic neoplasm, unclassified type
choices: Low grade oncocytic neoplasm, unclassified type
cases.histology: The tumor is well-circumscribed with a pushing border. Its architecture is variably solid or compact nests. Cytologically, there are large, round-to-polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with round to oval nuclei lacking irregularity surrounded by halos. Focally, there are myxoid areas with strands and individual cells.
cases.discussion:
Low Grade Oncocytic Tumor (LOT) is considered an “emerging tumor” in the latest 2022 WHO Classification. However, there are several series in the literature and in my experience, this is a well-established entity. It is rare and consequently most GU pathology experts who do not see a lot of renal tumor consults will have no experience with this entity, which has contributed to this lesion not being established as a definitive entity by the WHO. The main differential diagnoses is oncocytoma and chromophobe RCC. In contrast to oncocytoma, LOTs have a diffuse growth pattern as opposed to nests in oncocytoma. Although nuclei are uniform and round in LOT, similar to oncocytoma, LOTs have prominent perinuclear halos which are not seen in oncocytoma. Diffuse CK7 in LOTs would also rule out oncocytoma. While the perinuclear halos suggest chromophobe RCC, the round nuclei of LOT differ from the crinkled, notched, raisinoid nuclei of chromophobe RCC. Negative CD117 in LOT also differs from the diffuse membranous CD117 seen in chromophobe RCCs. Another characteristic feature of LOT that is not seen in oncocytoma or chromophobe RCC is what is described as an archipelago appearing myxoid matrix with cords of cells, some of which appear elongated and tethered with almost a tissue-culture appearance.

LOTs occur typically in adults with a wide age range. Tumors are usually unifocal, asymptomatic, and detected incidentally on imaging studies. LOTs are nonsyndromic. To date, LOTs have not exhibited malignant behavior, but there is insufficient data to claim they are totally benign. In addition to the characteristic CK7 diffuse positive with negative CD117, in our experience, LOTS have been diffusely positive for GPNMB, a marker associated with TSC/MTOR mutations, which have been found in LOTS. The term “LOT” is not well-known by urologists and can be misconstrued as a low grade oncocytic neoplasm that is not further classifiable. Consequently, when I diagnose LOT, I specify that this is a well-defined entity and give references on the lesion.

Reference: Hes O, Trpkov K. Do we need an updated classification of oncocytic renal tumors?: Emergence of low-grade oncocytic tumor (LOT) and eosinophilic vacuolated tumor (EVT) as novel renal entities. Mod Pathol. 2022 Sep;35(9):1140-1150.

Williamson SR, Hes O, Trpkov K, et al. Low-grade oncocytic tumour of the kidney is characterized by genetic alterations of TSC1, TSC2, MTOR or PIK3CA and consistent GATA3 positivity. Histopathology. 2023 Jan;82(2):296-304.

cases.histology: The tumor consists of a sieve-like (cribriform) growth pattern with a very irregular infiltrative border invading between glomeruli. The tumor has a moderate amount of eosinophilic cytoplasm with vesicular pleomorphic nuclei with prominent nucleoli. Frequent mitotic activity is noted. There is abundant dense desmoplastic stroma.
cases.discussion: Renal medullary carcinoma affects young adults, and is almost exclusively seen in Black patients with sickle cell trait. Inactivation of tumor suppressor gene hSNF5/INI1 on long arm of chromosome 22 is frequently detected. If there is morphology of medullary RCC and loss of INI1, but there is no history of sickle cell trait, it is termed INI-deficient RCC with medullary features. In this case, one can appreciate overt sickled cells in some of the vessels, so a definitive diagnosis of renal medullary RCC can be established. A typical feature of renal medullary RCC that is not prominent in the current case is the presence of microabcess formation and diffuse infiltration by neutrophils within the tumor. There is overlap with renal medullary RCC and collecting duct carcinoma. However, collecting duct carcinoma tends to have more individual tubules as opposed to a sieve-like growth pattern, and the clinical finding of sickle cell trait confirms the diagnosis of medullary RCC. Renal medullary RCC is associated with a very poor prognosis with >90% of patients at presentation having metastases to lymph nodes or other organs, with a median survival of 8 months.

This is a transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) specimen from a 57 year old male.
cases.feedback_text:
Sections show prostate tissue with a small focus of tubules lined by bland cuboidal epithelium, with admixed inflammation. Clear cell adenocarcinoma would typically form a mass lesion and should demonstrate mitotic activity as well as nuclear hyperchromasia, although shows extensive immunohistochemical overlap with nephrogenic adenoma. Urothelial carcinoma with glandular differentiation would typically label with GATA3 and lack PAX8 expression. Small vessels of granulation tissue can mimic tubules of nephrogenic adenoma, but these would label with endothelial but not epithelial markers.

The primary importance of nephrogenic adenoma, which represents colonization of the urinary tract (most commonly bladder or urethra) by shedding benign renal epithelial cells, is in not over diagnosing it as a neoplastic lesion. Diagnostic confusion may result from the presence of tubules in the bladder lamina propria and keratin labeling may also lead to concern for an epithelial neoplasm. The incidental nature, associated inflammation, hyaline cuff of basement membrane, lack of mitotic activity and nuclear hyperchromasia, and PAX8 labeling support this diagnosis.

cases.histology: The lesion is a relatively well-circumscribed and consists of a mixed inflammatory infiltrate that is notable for sheets of foamy, lipid-laden macrophages. Occasional multinucleated giant cells are also present. These histologic features support the diagnosis of xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, which is a distinct form of chronic pyelonephritis that occurs predominantly in pelvicalyceal areas.
cases.discussion: Neoplastic cells in clear cell renal cell carcinoma may mimic foamy macrophages; however, neoplastic cells stain positive for epithelial markers (e.g., AE1/3) and do not express macrophage markers (e.g., CD68 and CD163). Malakoplakia can present with similar histologic features as xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, but targetoid concentrically layered basophilic inclusions (Michaelis-Gutmann bodies) are characteristic of malakoplakia. Lastly, Rosai Dorfman disease is notable for macrophages with eosinophilic cytoplasm that stain positive for S100.

cases.histology: This neoplasm consists of atrophic, poorly formed glands with multilayered and basaloid nuclei with prominent nucleoli. By immunohistochemistry, the neoplasm demonstrates diffuse nuclear expression of p63 and expresses markers of androgen axis signaling in luminal cells, including androgen receptor (AR), NKX3.1, and prostein (P501S). This neoplasm also expresses prostate-specific antigen (PSA) and alpha-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR). Together, these findings support the diagnosis of prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression.
cases.discussion: Prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression typically shows diffuse nuclear expression of p63, and the absence of basal cells can be confirmed by the lack of expression of high molecular weight cytokeratin (HMWCK). In contrast, basal cell hyperplasia and basal cell carcinoma express HMWCK but do not show PSA positivity. Likewise, urothelial carcinoma does not express PSA, as well as P501S and NKX3.1. Prostatic adenocarcinoma with aberrant p63 expression is often mixed with conventional adenocarcinoma (85% of cases).

cases.source_answer: Papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity
cases.correct_answer: Papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity

choices_raw: Papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity
choices: Papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity
cases.histology: This neoplasm is well-circumscribed and shows predominantly papillary architecture with an arborizing proliferation of fibrovascular cores. Neoplastic cells are mostly cuboidal and have eosinophilic finely granular cytoplasm. Notably, their nuclei are located at the apical surface opposite to the basement membrane, and the overlying luminal borders are smooth in contour. The nuclei are also small with inconspicuous nucleoli. Psammoma bodies, intracellular hemosiderin, necrosis, tight clusters of foamy macrophages, and mitotic figures are absent. These findings support the diagnosis of papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity.
cases.discussion: While neoplastic cells in renal oncocytoma show abundant granular eosinophilic cytoplasm with uniform nuclei, renal oncocytoma typically exhibits solid nest architecture. Papillary renal cell carcinoma can exhibit papillary architecture, but the presence of nuclei that are located at the apical surface opposite to the basement membrane is characteristic of papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity. In addition, papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity stains positive for CK7 and GATA3 and negative for CA9. In contrast, papillary renal cell carcinoma does not express GATA3. MiT family translocation-associated renal carcinoma stains negative or is only focally positive for epithelial markers. Lastly, papillary renal neoplasm with reversed polarity is believed to be clinically indolent and is notable for KRAS missense mutations.

cases.histology: This neoplasm shows a solid and lobular growth pattern with fibrous bands. On higher power inspection, the neoplasm has multiple components, including formation of acini and squamoid nests. These areas of apparent acinar differentiation are predominant, consisting of relatively uniform cells with round nuclei and granular cytoplasm that are polarized around small lumina. These areas label for cytokeratins (CK8 and CK18), BCL10, trypsin, chymotrypsin, and lipase. Sqaumoid nests, which is required for this diagnosis, consist of whorled groups of plump squamoid cells. The squamoid nests show nuclear beta-catenin labeling.
cases.discussion: Squamoid nests are absent in acinar cell carcinoma, solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. While the patient in this case is an older female, pancreatoblastoma typically occurs in children (median age at diagnosis in children is 2.4 years). In contrast, acinar cell carcinoma, solid pseudopapillary neoplasm, and pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor usually occur in adults. In addition, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors lack acinar markers, and solid pseudopapillary neoplasm is negative for pancreatic enzymes, including trypsin and chymotrypsin.

cases.vignette: This is a 65 year old female with thickened gallbladder. A lesion is noted on the gallbladder serosa.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is a 65 year old female with thickened gallbladder. A lesion is noted on the gallbladder serosa.
cases.histology: The glandular proliferation is centered in the serosa of the gallbladder, which demonstrates fluid acute and chronic cholecystitis with ulceration and mural thickening. While the glands may appear irregular at high magnification, at low power one can appreciate that they are generally lobular and centered around larger ducts which focally have concentric fibrosis. The atypia is minimal, and mitotic features are not readily identified. These are the typical features of hyperplastic Luschka ducts, which are a recognized mimic of adenocarcinoma in the right upper quadrant fossa.
cases.discussion: Well differentiated adenocarcinomas may be extremely bland; however, one can expect to have more infiltrative growth, some greater degree of nuclear atypia, and perhaps perineural invasion. Collapsed liver can give a similar picture of proliferating bile ductules; however, in this case, the lesion is devoid of hepatocytes, and centered on the serosa of the gallbladder away from the liver. Adenomyosis is associated with herniation of biliary epithelium into the thickened gallbladder wall, and would consist of large sinuses and not proliferation of small ductules.

cases.vignette: This is a 40 year old male with a renal mass.
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Pedram Argani and prepared by Dr. Jae W. Lee.
This is a 40 year old male with a renal mass.
choices_raw: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor
choices: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor
cases.histology: This is a clear cell neoplasm with a solid nested architecture and central fibrosis, which correlates with its low nucleolar grade. On higher power inspection, one can appreciate that there is a tendency for the nuclei to be polarized away from the basement membrane, consistent with subnuclear vacuolization. Importantly, the stroma consists of highly vascularized septa, with prominent endothelial cells and minimal hyalinization. By immunohistochemistry, the neoplasm demonstrates diffuse membranous labeling for carbonic anhydrase 9 (CAIX) and CD10, and is essentially negative for cytokeratin 7. These findings support the diagnosis of clear cell renal cell carcinoma.
cases.discussion: The morphology of the neoplastic cells in this case overlaps with that of clear cell papillary cell tumor and TFE3 rearranged renal cell carcinomas, which frequently demonstrate subnuclear vacuoles when they harbor SFPQ-TFE3 or NONO-TFE3 gene fusions. TFEB-rearranged renal cell carcinomas also can closely mimic clear cell carcinomas and are in the morphologic differential diagnosis. The best clue to the diagnosis in this case is the high cellularity of the endothelium in the vascular septa, which strongly suggests a VEGF-driven neoplasm such as clear cell renal cell carcinoma which harbors VHL gene alterations. In this case, immunohistochemistry supports this interpretation, as diffuse CAIX labeling is not seen in translocation carcinomas and the CD10 immunoreactivity and absence of CK7 labeling argue against clear cell papillary renal cell tumor.

Invasive micropapillary carcinoma of the breast
cases.histology: This is an infiltrative neoplasm composed of nests of neoplastic cells with an “inside-out” growth pattern. Specifically, in many of the clusters, one can appreciate that the luminal surface is on the outside of the cluster rather than the inside as it would be in atypical gland. There is prominent space between the nests and the stroma, which is more prominent than seen in simple retraction artifact. Focally, one can appreciate an intermediate grade cribriform ductal carcinoma in situ component, assuring us that this is a primary breast neoplasm rather than a metastasis.
cases.discussion: Invasive lobular carcinoma would feature cords of bland neoplastic cells which permeate the stroma and lack e-cadherin immunoreactivity. Since greater than 90% of the tumor consists of morules of tumor cells with the inside-out growth pattern and stromal retraction, this neoplasm qualifies as a pure invasive micropapillary carcinoma rather than a ductal carcinoma of no special type. Metastatic ovarian carcinoma is excluded by the presence of a ductal carcinoma in situ. If this is not present, confirmatory stains for GCDFP and GATA 3 (positive) and PAX8 (negative) would support primary breast origin.

cases.feedback_text:
Sections show a malignant tumor metastatic to a lymph node. The tumor is cohesive and grows in large nests with peripheral palisading with comedo necrosis and rosette formation. Innumerable mitotic figures are seen. Paraganglioma is typically less cohesive appearing and would lack keratin expression. Well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumors are malignant and may be proliferative but lack this degree of extensive mitotic activity and comedo necrosis. Adenocarcinomas of various primary sites may show expression of neuroendocrine markers but lack the peripheral palisading and large solid nests with comedo necrosis. However, there may be substantial morphologic overlap between high grade adenocarcinoma and large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, and the latter may arise from the former and may predominate in metastatic sites due to its increased aggressiveness and proliferation rate. Because of the potential morphologic overlap between conventional adenocarcinoma and large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, strict criteria must be used to establish the latter diagnosis. First, neuroendocrine markers should only be applied if there are morphologic features concerning for large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (large nests with comedo necrosis and/or peripheral palisading, rosette formation). Further, unlike small cell carcinoma, which in certain instances can be diagnosed without immunohistochemistry documenting neuroendocrine differentiation, strong expression of multiple neuroendocrine markers in combination with the appropriate morphology, as demonstrated in this case, is required for the diagnosis of large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma.

Reference:

Corbett V, Arnold S, Anthony L, Chauhan A. Management of Large Cell Neuroendocrine Carcinoma. Front Oncol. 2021 Aug 27;11:653162. doi: 10.3389/fonc.2021.653162. PMID: 34513663; PMCID: PMC8432609.

cases.histology: Small foci in the mass are composed of sheets of cells, some with lumens, with markedly atypical nuclei containing multiple irregular nucleoli. Other foci have well-formed cytologically atypical glands surrounded by hypercellular atypical stroma with numerous mitotic figures. The majority of the tumor has a myxoid matrix and dilated glands with flattened epithelium. The surrounding testis focally shows germ cell neoplasia in-situ (GCNIS) within tubules that lack spermatogenesis. GCNIS is composed of a single layer of cells indistinguishable from seminoma cells surrounded by a halo. GCNIS always is seen in seminiferous tubules lacking spermatogenesis.
cases.discussion: In a post-pubertal type teratoma, there is no distinction between immature or mature teratoma. Also one does not note the presence of malignant cytology in the epithelial or stromal aspect of the teratoma unless these elements sheet out greater than 5 mm, at which point it becomes a somatic malignancy arising in a teratoma. It is not uncommon to have scattered teratoma glands that look like adenocarcinoma or where the surrounding stroma looks like a primitive sarcoma, but as long as these elements have not evolved into an expansile infiltrative carcinoma or sarcoma, then it has no significance and is just part of the post-pubertal type teratoma. The predominant component in this tumor is yolk sac tumor (YST). In this case the YST has a rare morphology composed of dilated cystic glands which is termed the polyvesicular vitelline pattern. In order to verify a yolk sac pattern one can use immunohistochemistry (IHC) for alpha feto protein (AFP). However, in patients with elevated serum AFP levels, IHC with AFP typically results in the entire tissue staining brown and is difficult to interpret. A better marker is glypican-3, which is a specific and sensitive marker for YST and is a much cleaner stain, where only the YST epithelium labels. Prognostically, once there is a malignant mixed germ cell tumor, the various proportions of the tumor elements are not important and the prognosis is determined by the levels of various serum markers and the stage of the tumor. The only situation where the composition of an organ-confined malignant mixed germ cell tumor could have implications is if the tumor is >50% embryonal carcinoma, which carries an increased risk of metastases to retroperitoneal lymph nodes.

cases.vignette: Case History: A 45 year-old male underwent a resection of a spermatic cord nodule. Diagnosis?
cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Jonathan Epstein and prepared by Dr. Eric Young.
Case History: A 45 year-old male underwent a resection of a spermatic cord nodule.
Diagnosis?
cases.histology: Adjacent to the vas deferens is a haphazard proliferation of tubules associated with fibrosis and hemosiderin deposition. The tubules have uniform nuclei with visible nucleoli.
cases.discussion: Vasitis nodosa typically results after vasectomy, where the cut ends of the vas deference proliferate as small tubules as a result of duct obstruction. The cut ends of the vas deferens are resected at the time of vasovasostomy, where microsurgery is performed to anastomose the ends of the vas deferens to reverse the vasectomy. Less commonly, prior surgery in this area other than vasectomy or trauma can injure the vas deferens and result in vasitis nodosa. Early on in the history of vasectomy there were cases of pregnancy after vasectomy as a result of these small tubules from each end of the cut surface of the vas deferens connecting up with each other. After recognition of this phenomenon, currently during vasectomy a piece of fascia is placed between the cut ends of the vas deferens to prevent this from happening. The tubules in vasitis nodosa are very proliferative and can show perineural invasion and even result in vascular invasion. In contrast to carcinoma, the tubules are cytologically bland, and In most cases, recognition of this entity is facilitated by the presence of sperm within the tubules and sperm granulomas, which result as a reaction to sperm. Due to the presence of prominent nucleoli and the location, metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma is the leading differential diagnosis, which can readily be ruled out with negative stains for NKX3.1, PSA, and P501S.

cases.question_text:

Case History: A 65 year old male underwent a partial nephrectomy for a 5.3 cm. cystic mass.
Diagnosis?
cases.source_answer: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor
cases.correct_answer: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor
cases.canonical_answer: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor
choices_raw: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor
Cystic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC)
Muticystic renal epithelial neoplasm of low malignant potential
choices: Clear cell papillary renal cell tumor
Cystic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (RCC)
Muticystic renal epithelial neoplasm of low malignant potential
cases.histology: Surrounding the cyst is a tubulopapillary neoplasm lined by cytologically bland epithelium with clear cytoplasm. Some of the tubules have reverse polarity where the nuclei are located towards the luminal surface with subnuclear clear cytoplasm.
cases.discussion: The morphology of this lesion is classic for a clear cell papillary renal cell tumor. It was formally called “clear cell papillary renal cell carcinoma”, but to date none of these lesions have exhibited metastases. It shows tubular and papillary growth patterns, which can vary in their proportion but typically is more tubular than papillary. In contrast, clear cell RCC typically has predominantly small solid nests of clear cells with an intervening rich thin capillary network. Many of the tubules in clear cell papillary renal cell tumor have blunt squared-off ends. Cytologically, the nuclei are always benign-appearing with in some areas showing reverse polarity, a feature that can vary in its prominence. Clear cell papillary renal cell tumors are typically solid, but can be cystic, as in this case, and can even uncommonly show cystic necrosis. Focally within a clear cell papillary renal cell tumor there may be areas that are indistinguishable from a low-grade clear cell RCC with small nests of clear cells separated by a thin vascular network. Similarly, within an otherwise typical clear cell RCC one can see focal areas resembling clear cell papillary renal cell tumor. Hence, one should assess what is the overall pattern of the tumor. Immunohistochemically, clear cell papillary renal tumor has a distinct staining pattern with diffuse CK7 and diffuse CAIX. The latter often has a “cup-shape” distribution, where the membranous CAIX staining is on the bottom and sides of the cells but not on the lumina surface (ie. not circumferential), resembling a goblet or chalice. This staining cup-like staining is not entirely specific or necessary for the diagnosis. A pitfall that many pathologists are not aware of is that low grade clear cell RCC can show a fair degree of CK7 positivity, yet will not be diffusely immunoreactive as in clear cell papillary renal cell tumor. In cases of clear cell papillary renal cell tumor with classic morphology, it is not necessary to stain with CK7 and CAIX, but the staining can be confirmatory if there is any uncertainty with the diagnosis. Multicystic renal epithelial neoplasm of low malignant potential (RCCLMP) is also cystic but multicystic, in contract to the current case. More importantly, RCCLMP consists of small solid non-expansile nests of what looks like low grade clear cell RCC in the septae of the cysts, in contrast to a cystic clear cell RCC, where there are expansile nests and larger solid areas in the cyst walls.

cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Lisa Rooper and prepared by Dr. Eric Young.
This is a 50-year-old male with a parotid mass.
Diagnosis?
cases.histology:
Here, we see a relatively well-circumscribed sclerotic and lobular nodule involving fibroadipose tissue, no normal parotid gland is apparent. The nodule features hypocellular mucinous areas of myxoid stroma and basophilic epithelioid cells in nests and vague duct-like structures. At higher power, the tumor cells have smooth nuclear borders and homogenous chromatin. These morphologic features are consistent with pleomorphic adenoma.

IHC: (+) p63, S100, keratins, GFAP

Molecular: rearrangements of PLAG1 or HMGA2

This specimen is from an 80-year-old male with a nasal mass.
Diagnosis?
cases.histology:
Here, we see fragments of sinonasal epithelium with an underlying mass comprised of plump basophilic and epithelioid and spindled cells arranged in loose whorls, thin-walled blood vessels with hyalinzation and extravasated blood. At higher magnification, we can see ovoid nuclei, pinpoint nucleoli, and fibrillary pink cytoplasm. These features are consistent with a sinonasal glomangiopericytoma.

IHC: (+) SMA, Beta catenin (nuclear), (-) CD34, S100, desmin, keratins

Molecular: CTNNB1 mutations (Beta catenin)

Here, we see a basophilic poorly circumscribed and infiltrative mass comprised of basophilic cells in lobules separated by what are revealed at high power as septae comprised of neural matrix. There is an irregular, thick fibrous capsule and no normal parotid is seen. At high power, the tumor cells are primitive appearing and basophilic with a high NC ratio, monomorphic, smudgy, salt and pepper chromatin arranged chromatin. This is consistent with metastatic olfactory neuroblastoma.

IHC: (+)synaptophysin, chromogranin (-)AE1/3

Differential diagnosis:

Neuroendocrine carcinoma (positive: AE1/3), Sinonasal undifferentiated carcinoma, lymphoma (positive: CD45), Ewing sarcoma, pituitary neuroendocrine tumor

Reference:

Fukushima S, Sugita Y, Niino D, Mihashi H, Ohshima K. Clincopathological analysis of olfactory neuroblastoma. Brain Tumor Pathol. 2012 Oct;29(4):207-15. doi: 10.1007/s10014-012-0083-3. Epub 2012 Feb 14. PMID: 22331316.

cases.question_text:
Case presented by Dr. Elizabeth Thompson and prepared by Dr. Eric Young.
This is a 60-year-old female with a colon polyp.
Diagnosis?
cases.histology:
Here, we see a portion of colon with areas of crypt distortion, paneth cell metaplasia, increased vascularity, creeping submucosal fat. eosinophilic stroma, and a conspicuous mass comprised of bland, spindled cells which is expanding the musculris mucosa. At higher power, lymphocytic infiltrate is observed with no apparent viral cytopathic effect or organisms. There is a notable onion skinning pattern of fibrosis around vessels and the histology is consistent with an inflammatory fibroid polyp.

IHC: (+) CD34

Molecular: PDGFRA mutations
